sorular.konu: LLM size and the memory problem (weights and KV cache)
sorular.soru: A 7B model's weights fit easily on a GPU, yet the server runs out of memory once it handles many users with long conversations. Which mechanism best explains this?
secenekler: The weights are copied once for each user, so weight memory grows in proportion to the number of open conversations
Longer prompts force the weights to be held at higher precision, so every extra token widens the weight format a little
Every new token adds keys and values in every layer for each user, so the cache grows while the weights stay fixed
Each step re-encodes all past tokens and keeps the results, so the temporary buffers end up outgrowing the KV cache
sorular.aciklama: The KV cache holds keys and values for every past token in every layer, separately for each user, so it scales with context length and user count and can outgrow the weights, whose size is fixed. The per-user copy option is wrong: the weights are shared by all conversations; only the cache is per user.

sorular.konu: Quantization basics: number formats, scale, and rounding
sorular.soru: A model is stored with weight-only INT4 quantization, and the integers are dequantized before each matrix multiplication. Why does this setup shrink memory use without automatically reducing the work done per token?
secenekler: Fewer bits are stored and moved per weight, but the same multiplications still run on the read-back values
Fewer weights remain after rounding, but the hardware cannot skip the removed ones without special sparse kernels
Fewer bits are stored per weight, but the activations and the KV cache must grow to absorb the rounding error
Fewer bits are stored per weight, but a short training run is needed at load time to restore the original values
sorular.aciklama: Quantization keeps every weight and only stores each one in fewer bits, which cuts storage and memory bandwidth; the number of operations is unchanged, and reducing compute requires quantizing activations as well. The sparse-kernel option describes pruning, which removes weights, whereas quantization keeps them all.

sorular.konu: The outlier problem, granularity, and calibration
sorular.soru: In a group of weights quantized to 4 bits with one shared scale, adding a single very large weight leaves that weight almost error-free but makes all the others far less precise. What is the mechanism behind this?
secenekler: The large weight exceeds the integer range, so it is clipped and its residual error is spread across the other weights
The scale is set by the largest magnitude, so the step widens and the normal weights collapse onto a few coarse levels
Rounding error is inversely proportional to magnitude, so weights with small absolute values inherently lose the most
The scale is unaffected; the loss comes from converting the integers back to floating point in the dequantize step
sorular.aciklama: With one scale derived from the largest |w|, an outlier stretches the grid so that it lands exactly on the top level, while the step becomes so wide that the ordinary weights round to zero or to one coarse level. The clipping option is wrong: nothing is clipped in this scheme; the outlier stays in range and harms the others by enlarging the step.

sorular.konu: The outlier problem, granularity, and calibration
sorular.soru: Two remedies for an outlier in quantized weights are giving each small group its own scale and clipping the range before the scale is chosen. How do the prices paid by these two remedies differ?
secenekler: Per-group scales sacrifice the outlier's value; clipping keeps the outlier exact but adds metadata and kernel complexity
Both keep every value exact; per-group scales cost a training run, whereas clipping only costs a small calibration set
Per-group scales raise the bit width of every weight; clipping lowers it, so only clipping still saves any memory
Per-group scales confine the damage but add metadata; clipping keeps common values precise but distorts the outlier
sorular.aciklama: With finer granularity the outlier spoils only its own small group, at the price of more stored scales and more complex kernels; a narrow clipped range keeps the common values precise, but the outlier is pulled to the edge of the range and alone carries a large error. The first option swaps the two costs.

sorular.konu: Weight / activation / KV-cache quantization and LLM.int8()
sorular.soru: What solution does the LLM.int8() work by Dettmers et al. (2022) offer against the collapse of plain 8-bit quantization from 6.7B parameters onward?
secenekler: Clipping all activations to |x| ≤ 6 and converting them to INT8 with a single per-tensor scale
Multiplying the few outlier feature columns with |x| > 6 in FP16 and the remaining >99.9% in INT8, then summing the two results
Pruning the weight columns that correspond to the outlier features and converting the remaining smaller matrix to INT8
Splitting the weights into groups of 128 and giving each group its own scale, so an outlier's effect is limited to its own group
sorular.aciklama: LLM.int8() splits the matrix multiplication in two: the very few outlier columns are computed in 16-bit and the rest in 8-bit, and the results are summed; this gives '8-bit memory, 16-bit quality' and matches the 16-bit curve even beyond 6.7B. Per-group scaling (the last option) is a genuine remedy for outliers, but it belongs to the general list of outlier remedies, not to the mechanism of LLM.int8().

sorular.soru: What is the usual division of labor between PTQ (post-training quantization) and QAT (quantization-aware training)?
secenekler: QAT is the first choice because it needs no calibration data; PTQ is reserved only for very low bit widths such as 2–3 bits
Both give the same quality; the difference is that QAT can also quantize the KV cache while PTQ is limited to weights
QAT is cheaper because it requires no extra training; PTQ needs a separate training run because it puts rounding into the training loop
PTQ is the first choice: it works well down to 4-bit with a small calibration set; QAT is for 2–3 bits and comes with a training cost
sorular.aciklama: PTQ is applied to a trained model with a small calibration set, is cheap, and works well down to 4-bit; QAT brings rounding into the training loop, so it costs a training run and is used when PTQ is not enough (2–3 bits). The third option reverses the roles: QAT is the one that requires training.

sorular.soru: In an LLM that has reached 50% unstructured sparsity, the number of nonzero parameters is halved, yet it is often warned that 'speedup is not automatic'. What is the reason for this warning?
secenekler: The zeros have no fixed pattern; dense kernels multiply the zeros too, so a gain requires special sparse kernels or the 2:4 pattern
Unstructured pruning can only be applied to the attention projections, so the computational load of the MLP layers stays entirely unchanged
The LoRA recovery step required after pruning adds an extra adapter multiplication to every layer at inference time, which cancels the speed gain
SparseGPT's δ updates put new nonzero values in place of the deleted weights, so the total number of operations actually does not change
sorular.aciklama: Unstructured sparsity has 'no fixed pattern; special sparse kernels needed': hardware cannot skip irregular zeros, so any speedup depends on hardware and kernel support, whereas structured pruning directly yields a smaller dense architecture and a speed gain is nearly guaranteed. The SparseGPT option is wrong: the δ updates are applied to the kept weights and do not change the sparsity ratio.

sorular.konu: Pruning scoring methods: Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT
sorular.soru: Under the same per-row pruning rule, Wanda keeps a small weight that magnitude pruning would remove and removes a larger one instead. What reasoning lies behind multiplying each weight's magnitude by the norm of its input?
secenekler: A removed weight's effect can be pushed into the remaining weights, so small weights become cheap to keep in the row
A weight fed by a strong input was trained for longer, so its magnitude is a more reliable estimate than the others
A weight's contribution to the output depends on its input too, so a small weight on a strong input can matter more
A weight on a strong input is enlarged by a short retraining pass, so its magnitude rises above the row threshold
sorular.aciklama: Magnitude pruning never looks at the inputs, yet what a weight adds to the layer output is the weight times its input; Wanda therefore scores each weight by |W| times the input norm measured on a few calibration texts. Pushing the effect of a removed weight into the remaining ones is SparseGPT's idea; Wanda neither updates weights nor retrains.

sorular.konu: Pruning scoring methods: Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT
sorular.soru: In a comparison of pruning methods on LLaMA-7B at 50% sparsity, what is the main difference between Wanda and SparseGPT?
secenekler: Wanda uses no calibration data while SparseGPT does; therefore SparseGPT's perplexity is clearly better
Both use calibration data; only SparseGPT updates the remaining weights with H⁻¹ to compensate for the error, and the ppl gap is small
Wanda updates the remaining weights while SparseGPT only selects what to remove; therefore their perplexities are nearly equal
SparseGPT performs a short retraining on labeled data, whereas Wanda settles for a single forward pass and is about 10 ppl points worse
sorular.aciklama: In the table, the 'calibration data' row is 'yes' for both Wanda and SparseGPT, while 'updates kept weights' is 'yes' only for SparseGPT; perplexities of 7.26 and 7.22 are nearly equal, a loss of ~1.5 points versus dense at 5.68. The method that uses no calibration data and loses ~11.6 points is magnitude pruning (17.29), not Wanda.

sorular.konu: Structured pruning, low-rank factorization, and recovery
sorular.soru: A team wants to run LLaMA-7B with genuinely lower latency on its own GPU; the hardware has no sparse kernel support, and memory is not a problem. A few hours of LoRA training are affordable. Which approach is the most appropriate?
secenekler: Apply 50% unstructured magnitude pruning and then recover the lost quality with LoRA
Convert the weights to weight-only INT4 and thereby automatically halve activation memory and compute cost as well
Define a smaller student architecture from scratch and train it with response-based distillation
Use structured pruning (e.g., LLM-Pruner, width/depth) to produce a smaller dense model and recover it with LoRA
sorular.aciklama: For real speed on your own hardware, structured pruning is the answer: when whole blocks, heads, or MLP neurons are removed, the model becomes smaller but stays dense, and no special kernel is needed; in an LLM-Pruner example, 20% of the structure is removed and ~3 hours of LoRA bring the score from 56.82 back up to 60.07. Unstructured pruning gives no speedup without sparse kernels; weight-only INT4 mainly targets memory and bandwidth and does not automatically reduce compute.

sorular.konu: Knowledge distillation: soft targets and temperature
sorular.soru: In the context of Hinton et al. (2015), what is meant by 'dark knowledge'?
secenekler: Internal representations hidden in the teacher's hidden states and attention features that are never reflected in the logit layer
Implicit knowledge about examples the teacher never saw in its training data, which can in no way be transferred to the student
The relative preference information in the small nonzero probabilities the teacher gives wrong classes (e.g., dog 0.018)
Knowledge the student acquires by discovering, on its own, patterns the teacher did not show, enabling it to surpass the teacher
sorular.aciklama: In soft targets, 'dog 0.018 ≠ 0' tells us the input also looks slightly like a dog, whereas a hard label says only 'cat'. The student thus learns the teacher's whole distribution, i.e., its relative preferences between classes. The first option describes feature-based KD; dark knowledge is the information in the output distribution (response-based).

sorular.konu: Knowledge distillation: soft targets and temperature
sorular.soru: In distillation, suppose the teacher gives 'cat 0.982 / dog 0.018' at T = 1 and '0.731 / 0.269' at T = 4. What is the rationale for using T > 1 in distillation?
secenekler: At T = 1 the distribution is almost one-hot, close to the hard label; T > 1 keeps the argmax but makes small probabilities visible
T > 1 changes the teacher's argmax; the student thus gives equal weight not only to the most probable class but also to the alternatives
T > 1 scales up the student's logits and thereby increases the gradient scale by τ², making training converge much faster
T > 1 filters out the teacher's low-confidence predictions; only the high-probability classes are transferred to the student
sorular.aciklama: Temperature divides every logit by T: the argmax does not change but the distribution flattens, so signals of 'dark knowledge' such as 0.018 reach a magnitude the student can learn (dog 0.401 at T = 10). The third option is wrong: T > 1 shrinks the gradient, and a τ² factor is added to the loss to compensate.

sorular.konu: KD loss and types of knowledge
sorular.soru: In the formula L_KD = α·L(W_S, x) + (1 − α)·τ²·KLdiv(Q_S, Q_T) used in knowledge distillation, what is the meaning of the τ² factor and of choosing α = 0?
secenekler: τ² softens the teacher output even further; α = 0 means the student learns only from the hard (true) labels, ignoring the teacher
τ² restores the gradient scale shrunk by softening; α = 0 switches off the label term, leaving only the teacher
τ² makes the KL divergence equivalent to cross-entropy; α = 0 disables the teacher term and uses only the ground truth
τ² balances the label and teacher terms; α = 0 indicates a switch from white-box KD to black-box KD in this setting
sorular.aciklama: When logits are divided by τ, gradients with respect to the soft targets shrink by roughly 1/τ²; the τ² factor restores this scale ('restores the gradient scale'). α balances labels against the teacher; α = 0 is the 'no labels' case and only the distillation term remains. The first and third options interpret α = 0 in reverse, as label-only.

sorular.konu: KD loss and types of knowledge
sorular.soru: TinyBERT copies not only the output probabilities but also the 'hidden layers'. Under the classification of Gou et al. (2021), which type of knowledge is this, and what is its prerequisite?
secenekler: Response-based; access to only the text the teacher generates or its token probabilities is sufficient
Relation-based; the similarity structure between examples or features must be taken from the teacher
Feature-based; access to the teacher's internal representations (white-box access) is needed
Black-box KD; the teacher behaves like an API and returns only softened probabilities
sorular.aciklama: Feature-based KD matches 'hidden states or attention features' and 'deeper knowledge gives a richer signal, but you need the teacher's internals'; TinyBERT's copying of intermediate layers is exactly this. Response-based KD uses only the teacher's predictions (probabilities / text) and does not need internal representations.

sorular.konu: KD case studies: DistilBERT/TinyBERT, Step-by-Step, Minitron
sorular.soru: In Distilling Step-by-Step (Hsieh et al., 2023), what happens when the student is deployed?
secenekler: The student first runs the [rationale] task to generate the rationale, then gives the final answer based on that rationale
The 540B PaLM teacher writes the rationale at test time, and the student derives the final answer from that rationale alone
The student uses only the [rationale] task; the answer is read from the last line of the generated rationale
Only the [label] task is used; at test time no rationale is generated and no large LLM is needed
sorular.aciklama: In training, the student learns two tasks on the same question with two prefixes ([label] → answer, [rationale] → rationale), and λ sets the weight of the rationale; at deployment only the answer task is used: 'no rationale and no LLM at test time'. The first option describes chain-of-thought inference; here the rationale is only a training signal and has no test-time cost.

sorular.konu: KD case studies: DistilBERT/TinyBERT, Step-by-Step, Minitron
sorular.soru: A company has trained a 15B-parameter model and now wants 8B and 4B variants of the same family, but it lacks the token budget to train each from scratch. Following the Minitron approach, what is the most efficient path?
secenekler: Prune the 15B model in width/depth and distill with the 15B as teacher; ~40× fewer tokens than training from scratch suffice
Quantize the 15B model to INT4 to match the memory footprint of 8B and 4B FP16 models; no additional training is needed
Collect the 15B model's rationales and train a small T5 from scratch with Distilling Step-by-Step; data needs drop to 80%
Randomly initialize the 8B and 4B architectures and train them with the 15B's soft targets; with no pruning, initial quality is preserved
sorular.aciklama: 'Train the biggest model once; get the smaller ones by pruning + distillation': the pruned model starts from trained weights and recovers quickly under teacher supervision, and Minitron 8B reaches the level of Mistral 7B / Gemma 7B with ~40× fewer tokens. A randomly initialized student (the last option) brings back exactly the 'from scratch' cost (40 units) that one wants to avoid; quantization does not change the parameter count and does not produce a separate 8B/4B architecture.

sorular.konu: KV-cache compression and choosing a method
sorular.soru: Quantizing the KV cache (e.g., KIVI) and evicting tokens from it (e.g., StreamingLLM, H2O) both reduce cache memory. How do the two approaches differ in what they give up?
secenekler: Quantization drops the oldest tokens entirely; eviction keeps all tokens but lets several query heads share one K/V head
Quantization shrinks the model weights that produce K and V; eviction removes whole layers so fewer entries are written
Quantization keeps every past token at lower precision; eviction keeps full precision but drops the middle of the context
Quantization keeps only the first and the recent tokens; eviction stores every token but with fewer bits for each entry
sorular.aciklama: Quantization lowers the bits per stored entry while every past token stays in the cache; eviction keeps the first ('sink') tokens and a recent window and discards what lies between. The last option swaps the two, and sharing one K/V head among several query heads is a third, separate lever (GQA).

sorular.konu: KV-cache compression and choosing a method
sorular.soru: In a LLaMA-7B / FreebaseQA experiment comparing GPTQ quantization with pruning (Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT), which conclusion can correctly be drawn?
secenekler: 8-bit GPTQ is lossless on this knowledge-heavy task; loss begins only at 4-bit, and even there it stays at the same level as 50% pruning
At the same 2× compression, 8-bit GPTQ is ≈ −10% while 50% pruning is −50% or worse; even 4-bit, at 4× compression, beats 2× pruning
Magnitude, Wanda, and SparseGPT stay in the green zone up to 50% sparsity; a marked collapse starts only beyond 60% sparsity
The pruning curves are flat up to 20–25% sparsity, and quantization causes more loss than pruning at every bit level
sorular.aciklama: In this experiment, 8-bit ≈ −10% and 4-bit ≈ −31%; pruning is fine up to 20–25%, then collapses and reaches −50% or worse at 50%, so at the same size quantization beats pruning. The first option is wrong: 8-bit is not free on knowledge-heavy tasks; even 8-bit shows a loss of ≈ −10%.
